content: 1. If a child is experiencing respiratory distress, assess their circulation. Look for signs such as cold skin, capillary refill time longer than 3 seconds, and a weak, rapid pulse. 2. If a foreign body is suspected to be aspirated, manage the airway according to the choking child protocol (Chart 3). If no foreign body is present, manage the airway as per Chart 4. 3. Administer oxygen as outlined in Chart 5 and ensure the child is kept warm. Stop any active bleeding. 4. If the child does not have severe malnutrition, insert an IV line and rapidly administer fluids as per Chart 7. If peripheral IV access is not possible, consider intraosseous or external jugular line placement. 5. For children with severe malnutrition who are lethargic or unconscious, administer IV glucose (Chart 10) and fluids (Chart 8). If the child is not lethargic or unconscious, provide glucose orally or via a nasogastric tube and proceed with a full assessment and treatment. 6. In cases of coma or convulsions, manage the airway (Chart 4). If convulsing, administer rectal diazepam (Chart 9). Position the unconscious child appropriately, stabilizing the neck if trauma is suspected (Chart 6). Administer IV glucose and ensure the child is kept warm. 7. For children with diarrhea and severe dehydration, assess for signs such as lethargy, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch, inability to drink, or poor drinking. Follow the appropriate dehydration treatment plan (Plan C for severe dehydration). 8. For choking infants, perform chest thrusts and back blows as per Chart 3. For older children, use the Heimlich maneuver and check for removable obstructions in the mouth. 9. To manage an obstructed airway in a child, inspect the mouth for foreign bodies, clear secretions, and position the child for optimal airway patency. If neck trauma is suspected, use a jaw thrust maneuver to open the airway while stabilizing the neck. 10. Administer oxygen via nasal prongs or a nasal catheter, ensuring proper placement and securing with tape (Chart 5). 11. Position unconscious children carefully. If neck trauma is suspected, stabilize the neck and keep the child lying on their back. If no neck trauma is suspected, turn the child on their side to reduce aspiration risk (Chart 6). 12. For children in shock without severe malnutrition, administer IV fluids rapidly (20 mL/kg) using Ringer’s lactate or normal saline. Reassess after each infusion and adjust treatment based on the child’s response (Chart 7). 13. For children with severe malnutrition and shock, administer IV fluids cautiously (15 mL/kg over 1 hour) and monitor closely for signs of improvement or complications such as pulmonary edema (Chart 8). 14. If a child is convulsing, administer rectal diazepam based on weight. If convulsions persist, consider phenobarbital or phenytoin. For high fever, undress the child to reduce temperature and avoid oral medications until convulsions are controlled (Chart 9). 15. For hypoglycemia, administer 10% glucose solution IV (5 mL/kg) and recheck blood glucose after 30 minutes. If still low, repeat the glucose bolus. Feed the child as soon as they are conscious, using oral or nasogastric feeding if necessary (Chart 10). 16. For severe dehydration after initial shock management, switch to oral rehydration salts (ORS) as soon as the child can drink. Reassess hydration status regularly and adjust treatment accordingly (Chart 11). 17. Monitor vital signs such as pulse rate, respiratory rate, and capillary refill time to assess for shock. Use systolic blood pressure ranges appropriate for the child’s age to confirm shock if necessary. 18. Evaluate the child’s mental status using the AVPU scale (Alert, Verbal response, Pain response, Unresponsive) to assess for coma or abnormal neurological status.
